first.rationale: Simplifying onboarding directly addresses the concurrent declines in onboarding completion and activation, with two inherited records indicating durable gains in activation, completion, time-to-value, and early adoption. It is preferable to promotional pricing despite competitive pressure because pricing previously harmed 30-day retention. Verification should confirm the durability and downstream quality of the onboarding results; qualified-revenue impact remains uncertain.

mid.rationale: Run a controlled onboarding-simplification experiment. The verified evidence directly addresses both current declines: shortened onboarding raised completion 13%, reduced time-to-value by 2.1 days, and improved 30-day retention 3%; SMB signup simplification raised activation 9% and qualified revenue 4%. A standard experiment is preferable to broad rollout because the signup result was limited to SMBs and showed a 1% retention decline. Promotional pricing is rejected despite competitive pressure because prior evidence found material retention harm.

final2.rationale: Maintain the onboarding-simplification experiment. Verified evidence shows gains in completion, activation, qualified revenue, time-to-value, and retention, directly addressing the current operational declines. The deeper competitor discount increases urgency but does not reverse the known downside of promotional pricing: it produced acquisition and revenue lift while materially reducing 30-day retention. That tradeoff conflicts with sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and price-related churn conversations alone do not establish that another discount would improve net retention. Keep the test controlled because signup simplification was validated only for SMBs and showed a small retention decline.
